turns.input: *i open my eyes and wander to the forest opposite of the big city in front of me*
turns.reply:
A cart rattles past on the road behind, the driver not so much as turning his head — one more traveler with freight and no interest in a stranger loitering on the verge.

The forest takes him in under a bough of old oaks. Ground that held road-dust for three steps now gives soft and spongy, leaf-rot dark enough to stain a boot. The wind drops once inside; what replaces it is birdsong in short, territorial bursts, and somewhere the knocking of a woodpecker working a dead trunk.

This is no wilderness. Ten minutes in, the trees start carrying marks: a beech stump cut two seasons back and again at the regrowth, a rope snare strung across a rabbit run with the hair of some failed catch still caught in the noose. The snares have been checked recently — the leaf litter around the pegs is disturbed, boot-shaped, a day old at most. Somebody works this wood for a living, and works it often.

Farther in, the ground climbs into a shallow ridge, and through the trunks comes a sound with weight to it: an axe, one stroke every few seconds, unhurried, the rhythm of a man splitting firewood rather than felling timber. Between strokes there's a second sound — a voice, low, talking. To no one. A monologue, muffled by distance, the words not carrying, only the cadence of somebody who has gotten into the habit of arguing with himself.

The axe stops mid-stroke.

The silence after it holds for a long moment — then, from the same direction, footsteps, deliberate, moving.

turns.input: *i follow the sounds bow ready as i openly walk towards the voice*
turns.reply:
"That's far enough."

The voice comes from downhill and to the left, older, roughened — a man's voice that has spent years carrying over wind. Its owner rises out of the bracken on the ridge's far side like he's been standing there a while: broad through the shoulders, narrow through the legs, a hand-axe hanging from his belt and a leather apron dark at the thighs with sap and old blood. Grey stubble. A face weathered down to the grain. In one hand, a dead rabbit by the ears.

The rabbit is fresh. So is the look he gives the bow.

He doesn't reach for the axe. He plants his feet instead and lets the carcass dangle, and his eyes go from the bow to the quiver to the clothes under the armor — the clothes of a town, or no trade he can name — and back to the bow.

"Point that down, lad. Ground rules." He hooks a thumb toward the snare line, the pegs, the cut stumps beyond. "My line. Eleven years I've run it. Every beast in this wood knows my boots better than its own mother."

He starts forward — unhurried, deliberately loud, each step cracking a stick on purpose so there's no mistaking where he is. He stops a dozen paces off. Close enough to talk. Far enough to swing the axe if it comes to that.

"Now. Either you're lost, or you're hunting on my ground without asking." He lifts the rabbit a little, as evidence, as punctuation. "Third one this season comes creeping up my ridge with a strung bow. First two got sent back to Tidecross the short way."

A pause. He shifts the rabbit to his other hand, wipes his palm on the apron.

"So which is it. Talk."

**Name:** Bram Fenn | **Age:** 57 | **Sex:** M | **Orientation:** Widower; not a plot matter

**Role:** Trapper and firewood-cutter working the eastern forest outside Tidecross

**Where to Find Them:** His trapline on the eastern ridge, or his cabin deeper in the wood; sells rabbits and cords of wood at the Tidecross gate market most market days

**Appearance:** Broad-shouldered, narrow-hipped, moving like a man half his age on ground he knows. Grey stubble, deep weathered lines, hands scarred at the knuckles from wire and hatchet work. Wears a sap-and-blood-darkened leather apron over wool. Deliberately loud on purpose, silent when he chooses.

**Image Tags:** 1boy, solo, male, grey hair, short hair, stubble, grey eyes, weathered skin, tan skin, muscular, broad shoulders, aged male, scarred hands, facial scar, wrinkle

**Voice:** Roughened rural Solmere drawl; drops word-endings; talks in short declaratives and rules ("ground rules," "my line"). Mutters half-sentences to himself when he thinks nobody's listening — a habit that has outlived its reason. Dodges nothing so directly as questions about the cabin.

**Background:** Born in a fishing hamlet up the coast, came inland with a wife and nothing else forty years back. Cut timber, ran snares, raised one daughter who married a cooper in Tidecross and visits less each year. The wife died eight winters ago; the talking-to-himself started that same winter and never stopped. He claims the eastern ridge as his ground by eleven years of work, though whether the wood is truly his to claim is a question he answers with the axe handle. The two poachers he mentions were handled — the details of how are his to keep.

**Inner Circle:**
* Maren Fenn — deceased wife | d. eight years ago; the reason he talks to the trees
* Sela Fenn — daughter | 34, cooper's wife in Tidecross; estranged by slow drift, not quarrel
* Osric Hale — Tidecross gate-market cordwood buyer | 48; owes Bram money, avoids him

**Personality:**
* Defining traits: territorial generosity — shares rabbit with the hungry, shares his wood with no one; loud on approach, silent by instinct
* Core flaw: treats every armed stranger as a poacher until proven otherwise, and proof is on his terms only
* Core fear: being pushed off the ridge — the last thing that is his
* Tell: when lying, he re-grips whatever he's holding and looks at the ground, not the listener

**Read on the PC:** A town-clothed stranger with a strung bow walking openly up his ridge — reads him first as poacher, possibly as something worse. Could soften fast if the bow comes down and the tongue works; could turn ugly if it doesn't.

**Agenda:** Get the bow lowered, get a name and a reason, get back to his line before the afternoon snares go stale.

**Secrets:**
* Tier 1 (semi-public): Tidecross hunters know his ridge is bad ground to poach — stories about the "short way back"
* Tier 2 (private): The two poachers this season weren't just chased off — one left gear behind that Bram still has, gear he can't place any known maker on
* Tier 3 (buried): The one-sided talking started the winter his wife died, and some of it isn't habit — he answers things out here, sometimes, and doesn't like to examine what with

turns.input: Lost *i say calmly as i lower my Bow ready to turn around and continue hunting*
turns.reply:
The rabbit thumps against Bram's thigh as he shifts it to his belt, and he watches the bow come down the way a man watches a snake lower its head — glad of it, unconvinced.

"Lost." He turns the word over once, spits into the leaves. "Lost men find a road. Lost men don't climb a ridge with a strung bow an' a full quiver."

He doesn't move to stop him, though. Feet planted, arms settling into a fold, he lets the silence do a share of the work while the stranger turns away. The birds have started up again in the canopy, short territorial bursts, and somewhere downhill the woodpecker is back at its dead trunk.

"Oi." A stick cracks under his boot, loud on purpose. "You huntin', then — fine. Wood past the stream's none of mine. Deer cross at the fallen birch, evenin' mostly, dawn if the frost is thick." He hooks a thumb back over his shoulder, toward the deeper ridge. "Everything this side of the water is snare ground. Fur in a snare is my supper. I count 'em, lad. Every one."

He waits long enough for that to land, then turns back down his line without a goodbye, the hand-axe swinging easy at his hip. His boots are loud going out, loud the way he chooses to be loud.

Ten paces on, the loudness stops. What carries instead is the murmur — that one-sided talk, pitched low, half to the trees, half to whatever answer he expects from them. One fragment rides the still air far enough to catch:

"—third one this season, an' the year's barely —"

The rest is lost under distance. Then the axe resumes, one stroke every few seconds, unhurried, and the ridge closes up behind the sound.

Cold comes up off the water before the water itself is visible — the air changing taste a full minute before the stream shows through the trees, carrying the mineral smell of stone run over by snowmelt.

The trail earns itself slowly. A browse line on the holly, clipped neat at head-height. Droppings gone grey and dry, then a second pile, darker, still holding shine — this morning's. Hoofprints pressed into the soft ground between the roots, split-toed, deep at the heel: an animal moving unhurried, feeding as it went. The tracks braid together with older ones and older ones beneath those, a road worn into the wood by generations of the same feet, and behind it all the axe strokes fade until the ridge is quiet except for a jay somewhere overhead, scolding at nothing, working its way tree to tree in the same direction as the trail.

The ground drops. Ferns replace the bracken, and then the stream is there — narrow, quick, brown water corded over gravel, loud enough to cover a footstep on either bank. Downstream, forty paces, a birch lies fallen across the water, its crown matted into the far bank. Exactly where the old man said it would be.

The mud at the water's edge is printed thick with last night's traffic. Deer, several, coming down to drink in the dark. But nearer the fallen trunk something else sits in the brush: a wire snare, sprung, its peg ripped clean out of the ground, hung up grey and weathered in the low branches. The wire is heavier gauge than the nooses on the ridge. Whoever set it wanted to hold something bigger than rabbits, and it snapped under the trying. A hand-span above it, a blaze is cut into an oak's bark — two short slashes, healed over dark with sap, old work. The kind of mark a man cuts so he can find his own way back to a place he has no right to be.

The wind shifts upstream, off the water, and brings a thread of something with it. Woodsmoke. Thin, days-old in its own way — a fire banked and tended, living somewhere down that stretch of the stream where the trees thicken into shadow.

On the far bank, the freshest tracks lead away from the water and downstream. Toward the smoke.

turns.input: *i follow the tracks towards teh smoke sneaking as i crouch and walk silently*
turns.reply:
The stream does half the work — brown water loud over gravel, loud enough to drown a boot placed careful in cold mud. The near bank holds its shadow under the ferns, and the deer tracks run clean in it, downstream, toward the smoke.

"Funny kind of lost."

The voice comes from behind. Close. Ten paces, no more, and no stick cracked to announce it — the man who was loud all morning by choosing to be has crossed a quarter mile of his own wood without a sound.

Bram stands off the trail with a coil of wire in one hand, snares from his morning round, and he isn't leaning on anything. The hand-axe hangs at his hip with his thumb hooked loose near the haft.

"Saw you from the birch. You bent your back the moment you thought the ridge was done with you." He lets that sit. The stream fills it. "Lost men ask directions. Lost men walk the road an' wave at a man workin'. You went quiet."

He comes a step nearer, boots deliberate now, loud on purpose again, and stops where the fern thins. His eyes go past — downstream, to the fallen birch, to the thread of smoke riding the tree-shadow — and come back.

"That fire's been down there three weeks. Man keeps to it. I keep to my side of the water, an' we've had no quarrel." A pause. He shifts the wire coil to his other hand. "That sprung wire back up the trail ain't mine. Heavy gauge. Somebody wanted to hold somethin' with hooves an' lost it. Third stranger this season walks my ridge, an' now a fourth goes creepin' toward that camp like he's scoutin' it."

He plants his feet. The rabbit-snare smell comes off the wire in his hand, blood and cold fur.

"So we'll do this proper, since you like the quiet." His voice drops, flattens out. "Name. What you're about on my water. Then you turn back up the trail, or you go down there —" a nod, downstream, toward the smoke "— an' whatever finds you down that stretch finds you without me comin' after it."

His thumb settles on the axe haft. Not gripping. Just resting there, the way a man rests a hand on a fence post he built himself.

turns.input: *i turn and say* how about you take that here and leave me alone and i leave your side of the water alone *i say and throw a silver coint to him*
turns.reply:
The coin spins through the space between them, catching what light the canopy lets down — and Bram's hand comes up and takes it out of the air the way a man catches a wasp. No fumble. Scarred fingers close around the silver and hold it flat on his palm, and he looks at it for a long moment like it's something he's found under a rock.

Then his arm moves and the coin comes back, low and hard, and lands in the mud a hand's width from Alaric's boot.

"Pick that up." He doesn't raise his voice. The wire coil goes down on a stone beside him, slow, deliberate, both hands free now. "I don't sell my ground. Not to you, not to the cooper's man that owes me an' hides when I walk the market. Not to anybody."

He comes two steps closer, boots loud in the fern, and stops with the stream loud between them.

"An' think on what you just did, lad. Man offers coin to be left alone, that man's got a purpose he don't want spoke." His thumb finds the axe haft again and this time it stays. "First two this season, they wanted the wood. Deer, rabbit. I sent 'em off an' that was the end of it. You want past me, toward that fire." A nod, downstream, at the thin thread of smoke. "That's different. That's business."

The jay is still working the canopy overhead, scolding. Under it, the water cords over its gravel, brown and quick.

"So here's how it stands now. You pick up your silver. You give me a name — any name, I don't care if it's your mother's — an' you tell me plain what you want down that stretch." He shifts his weight off the bad knee, settling in. "Or you walk back up the trail the way you came, an' we forget the coin ever left your pouch."

He waits. He's good at it — a man who spends whole mornings watching a wire.

"Third one this season," he mutters, half to the trees, half to nobody. "Fourth, rather. An' this one carries money."

turns.input: My name is *i begin to distract him and then i suddenly aim and Power Shot at him*
turns.reply:
"My name is—"

The draw cuts the name in half. The bow comes up off the hip where it hung, full draw in a breath, and the release is ugly-fast — Power Shot, everything behind it, the string slapping the bracer hard enough to sting through the sleeve. The arrow goes low and wide, hissing past Bram's hip and burying itself in the fern bank behind him with a sound like a door slammed in another room.

Eight paces off, the old man hasn't moved. Not a flinch, not a step — the wire coil still on the stone beside him, the axe still at his hip, and the space where the arrow passed shows a hand's width of air between his thigh and where he stood a half-second before.

He looks down at the fletching sticking out of the ferns. Then up.

"You SHOT at me." The flat calm is gone all at once, and what's under it is louder and older than anything he's used so far. "On MY water. After coin, after —" His hand comes off the axe haft and he points, finger shaking, at the arrow, at the stranger, back at the arrow. "Forty years in this wood an' nobody — NOBODY —"

He stops himself. Breathes through his nose, once, the way a man does when there's wire in his hands and a lifetime of knowing what rushing costs. His feet don't move. His weight stays settled, bad knee and all, but something in the set of his shoulders has changed — the deliberate loudness gone out of him entirely, and what's left is the other man, the quiet one, the one the rabbits never hear.

"That's how it is, then." Low now. Almost gentle. "That's how you want it."

His hand comes back to the axe. The jay goes up out of the canopy in a clatter and the stream keeps on over its gravel, brown and quick, indifferent to both of them.

turns.reply:
The second arrow takes him in the meat of the left shoulder, high, punching through the apron and out the back of the wool beneath it.

The sound he makes isn't a scream. It's shorter than that — a bark, punched out of him, the kind of noise a man makes when a maul bounces back off a knot. His whole left side jerks. The wire coil goes over on the stone. He staggers a half-step and catches it, and the rabbit-snare smell of the apron is suddenly mixed with the copper of new blood, sharp on the cold air coming off the water.

He doesn't charge.

That's the thing — eight paces of open fern between them, an axe on his hip, a man half his age with the bow already leveling again, and Bram Fenn does not charge. His right hand closes on the shaft and snaps it off clean a hand below the barbs, and he does it looking at the bow the whole time, not at the broken arrow. Then he moves — sideways, quick for a bad-kneed man of fifty-seven, and puts the blazed oak between his body and the water. Bark and old sap at his back. One shoulder of him showing at the edge of the trunk, and that shoulder is the unwounded one, and the hand holding the axe comes off his hip easy as breathing.

"Wounded me," he calls from behind the oak. His voice has gone back to level — the rage packed down under it somewhere, load-bearing now. "Forty years, an' the first blood on this ridge in eleven years is mine. You notice that, do you."

A pause. The stream talks over it. Somewhere down the far stretch, faint, a branch cracks — nothing that answers to a name, just the wood going about its morning around two men who have stopped being part of it.

"First two this season, I ran off." The words come around the trunk, unhurried, the way he talks to the trees. "You I'm not runnin' anywhere. Man shoots twice, he's past talkin'. So you just stand there an' think, lad. You've got the reach on me. I've got the wood."

The axe head gleams once at the trunk's edge, and is gone.

turns.reply:
The third arrow takes him where the second didn't — the right shoulder, the one he'd been showing at the trunk's edge, the one doing all the work. The shaft punches in above the collarbone and the whole arm drops dead to his side, and this time the sound is just air, shoved out, a man's breath leaving through his teeth.

The shoulder vanishes behind the oak. Both of him does.

Then, muffled through the trunk, the voice — thinner now, pulled tight across the wound.

"Still shootin'. No name. No —" A stop. A sound like swallowing. "Aye. Fine."

Under it, lower, the half-talk comes out anyway, the habit outliving its reasons: "Two arms gone stupid. Lovely. Maren, you'd laugh —" The name cuts off like a door pulled shut, and after that there's only working sounds: a knee settling into the dirt, the rasp of wool, the wet drag of a strap pulled through teeth one-handed.

Blood has found the ground around the trunk's base. It runs the bark seam down the oak and pools in the root-flare, black in the canopy shade, and it keeps coming — slower than a butcher's spill, steady as a tapped keg. The stream goes on over its gravel ten paces off, and the woodpecker has started up again somewhere up the ridge, knocking at its dead trunk like nothing on this water has changed.

From behind the oak, one more thing, pitched to carry:

"I know this ground, lad. Every foot of it. You've got arrows. I've got patience." A pause, and the strain under it. "Come see which runs out first."

Then nothing. Just the blood, finding its way down through the fern roots, and the oak standing between them like a wall with a wounded man packed behind it.
